items.rationale:
- Workflow: code decides which step runs next. Agent: the model decides it.
- a: workflows use tools too (M7, tools make it an agent).
- b: both designs use a model (M8, a workflow has no model).
- d: call count follows from who decides; it is not the test (M11, more calls means agent).

- Code owns the loop: it runs the check, decides to retry and sets the cap of 3. That makes it a workflow.
- a: a loop alone does not make an agent; who controls it does (M14, any loop means agent).
- c: the model writes content but does not choose the steps (M13, the model doing the work means it owns the flow).
- d: nothing here is split; code decides every step (M12, a loop makes a third category).

- Booking has known steps in the same order every time, so code can run them: cheaper, faster, more predictable.
- a: repeated searching still follows a known pattern, but the number of rounds depends on results (M15, iterative search needs an agent).
- b: the next check depends on the student's answers (M16, anything conversational needs an agent).
- c: which sources to look at depends on the description (M17, bigger tasks need an agent).
- In a, b and c the path depends on what comes back, which is where an agent pays off.

- A fixed workflow only handles paths written into the code, so you give up flexibility for requests nobody anticipated.
- b, c: a workflow can use tools and a model (M7, M8).
- d: predictable cost is what a workflow gains, not loses (M18, a workflow's cost is less predictable than an agent's).

items.answer: Code runs a fixed, known number of steps, so there are fewer model calls and none spent on deciding what to do next, while an agent's number of calls varies.
accepted: The workflow has a known, fixed number of model calls, while an agent makes a variable number as it decides its own steps
An agent spends extra model calls deciding what to do next; a workflow's code already knows the steps
A workflow makes fewer and more predictable model calls because code, not the model, decides the steps
Fewer model calls, because the steps are fixed in code
items.rationale:
- Cost follows model calls. In a workflow, code sets the steps, so the count is small and known.
- An agent spends calls choosing its next action and may loop longer, so cost is higher and varies.
- 'Workflows use a cheaper model' or 'workflows skip tools' is not the reason.

- Control flow can be split: the code rule constrains the order of those two tools; the model still chooses everything else.
- a: the rule now overrides the model for that ordering (M19, a code rule changes nothing about who decides).
- b: one rule does not make every step code-decided (M20, one fixed rule makes the whole system a workflow).
- d: mixing is normal; the two are ends of a spectrum (M10, a system is wholly one or the other).
